body:
Origin and introduction

The Ryotwari Settlement was developed as an alternative to the zamindari-based arrangement of the Permanent Settlement.

It was first tried on a limited scale by Captain Alexander Read in southern Indian territories acquired by the Company after wars with Tipu Sultan. These experiments began during the closing years of the 18th century.

The system was subsequently developed and extended by Thomas Munro, who served as Governor of Madras during 1820–1827.

Ryotwari became particularly associated with the Madras and Bombay Presidencies, although its precise administrative arrangements were not identical in every district.

Meaning of Ryotwari Settlement

Under the Ryotwari Settlement, the government assessed land revenue with reference to the holding of an individual cultivator, or ryot, who was directly responsible for paying the assessed revenue to the state.

Unlike the Permanent Settlement, there was no zamindar placed between the ryot and the government as the principal estate-level revenue payer.

The Ryotwari arrangement was based on the view that, in many southern regions, cultivators held established rights over the land they had traditionally cultivated and that revenue settlement should be made directly with them.

How revenue was assessed and collected

The government attempted to determine the assessment of individual holdings through surveys and examinations of agricultural conditions.

  1. Measurement of holdings: Officials identified and measured the agricultural fields associated with individual cultivators.
  2. Examination of productive capacity: Soil quality, cultivation and estimated agricultural output were considered in assessing the land.
  3. Determination of demand: The government fixed the revenue payable by the ryot according to the assessment.
  4. Direct payment: The cultivator became responsible for paying the assessed revenue to the government through its revenue administration.
  5. Subsequent reassessment: Unlike the Permanent Settlement, the assessment could be revised according to the applicable settlement arrangements.

Rights of the cultivator

Under the Ryotwari arrangement, the individual cultivator was recognised as the principal holder of the assessed land and was generally granted legally recognised occupancy or proprietary rights, subject to the applicable revenue and land laws.

These rights could include continued occupation, inheritance and transfer of holdings, subject to relevant conditions. However, the cultivator's right was not unconditional: payment of government revenue remained an important obligation.

Written revenue documents, including pattas, could record the cultivator's holding and the associated assessment.

Direct settlement did not mean freedom from taxation or absolute ownership without conditions. The cultivator still had to satisfy the government's revenue demand, and the extent of landholding rights depended on the rules applicable in the region.

Was the revenue permanently fixed?

No. The Ryotwari Settlement generally involved periodically revisable revenue assessments.

Under the system used in the Bombay Deccan, the land was resurveyed at intervals of approximately 30 years, after which revenue rates could be reassessed. This was a feature of that regional arrangement, not a uniform settlement period that applied to every Ryotwari district throughout British India.

Officials could therefore alter the government's demand when a settlement was revised. This distinguished Ryotwari from the permanent revenue assessment of Bengal.

Effects on cultivators

The elimination of the zamindar as the principal revenue intermediary did not automatically protect cultivators from economic hardship.

Revenue assessments could be extremely high. In areas with poor soil, uncertain rainfall or low agricultural prices, cultivators often struggled to pay.

Because revenue had to be paid to the government, many ryots depended on private moneylenders for credit. Failure to repay loans could result in growing indebtedness and loss of effective control over land.

In parts of the Bombay Deccan, high assessments during the 1820s contributed to financial distress, migration and the abandonment of some villages. Revenue officials subsequently recognised that some earlier demands had been excessive.

Moneylenders and revenue officials could exercise considerable power over cultivators even though the formal settlement was made directly between the ryot and the state.

Principal distinction from the Permanent Settlement

Under the Permanent Settlement, the government looked to the zamindar for payment of a permanently fixed estate-level demand.

Under Ryotwari, the individual cultivator was the principal person assessed for revenue, and the government's demand was capable of periodic revision.

Prelims focus

  • Alexander Read: Associated with the early Ryotwari experiments.
  • Thomas Munro: Developed and extended the system in the Madras Presidency.
  • 1820–1827: Munro's tenure as Governor of Madras.
  • Major regions: Madras and Bombay Presidencies.
  • Principal revenue payer: Individual ryot.
  • Trap: The absence of a zamindar intermediary did not mean that ryots were free from debt, revenue pressure or official control.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, section The Munro System, printed pp. 29–30, 2020–21 edition in GPSC Volume 04; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Theme 9, sections 3.2–3.3, printed pp. 247–249, online 2024–25 edition consulted 20 November 2026; Drishti IAS, Land Revenue Systems in British India, section The Ryotwari System, published 7 December 2020, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Ryotwari Settlement: Direct Revenue Collection from Individual Cultivators

body:
Origin of the Mahalwari Settlement

The Mahalwari Settlement was introduced in 1822 in the North-Western Provinces of the Bengal Presidency, much of which corresponds to areas of present-day Uttar Pradesh.

The system was devised by Holt Mackenzie, who considered the village an important institution in northern Indian society.

The arrangement was subsequently modified during British administration, including changes introduced in 1833 under Lord William Bentinck.

Mahalwari arrangements became associated with the North-Western Provinces and were adopted in forms in other northern and northwestern territories, including parts of Punjab.

Meaning of a mahal

In colonial land revenue administration, a mahal was a revenue estate that could consist of a single village or a group of villages.

Under the Mahalwari Settlement, the principal revenue assessment was made for the mahal rather than establishing the government demand solely through an individual cultivator, as in Ryotwari, or through a permanently assessed zamindari estate, as in the Permanent Settlement.

The term mahal referred to a revenue unit. It did not necessarily mean one village, and its use in a historical document does not by itself establish that the Mahalwari system operated there.

How the system operated

The Mahalwari Settlement combined detailed land assessment with recognition of village-level institutions and rights.

  1. Survey of agricultural land: Revenue officials visited villages, inspected fields and measured cultivated land.
  2. Recording of rights: Officials investigated local customs and the rights of individuals and groups associated with the land.
  3. Assessment of plots: Estimated revenue was determined for the separate plots within the revenue estate.
  4. Assessment of the mahal: Individual assessments were combined to determine the total revenue demand of the mahal.
  5. Collection and payment: The village headman or recognised representatives arranged collection and payment of the assessed revenue to the government.
  6. Periodic revision: The settlement could be reassessed after the applicable settlement period.

Village responsibility and landholding rights

The Mahalwari Settlement generally recognised the role of village communities, co-sharers or other locally established holders of rights over the land.

The village headman, sometimes described in revenue administration as a lambardar or recognised revenue representative, had responsibility for organising collection and payment.

In many Mahalwari arrangements, the recognised village proprietors or co-sharers bore joint responsibility for the government's revenue demand.

This collective responsibility distinguished Mahalwari from Ryotwari. Although individual fields could be separately surveyed, the government's principal settlement unit was the mahal.

Joint revenue responsibility did not necessarily mean that every field was owned collectively or that each cultivator possessed identical rights. Individual and family claims could continue within the wider revenue estate.

Was the revenue permanently fixed?

No. Mahalwari revenue demands were revisable at periodic settlements.

Unlike the Permanent Settlement, the government could revise the assessment after examining the applicable revenue conditions. This allowed the colonial administration to reconsider its claim on agricultural income.

Effects on village communities

The system was intended to preserve the role of village institutions while providing an organised method of revenue assessment.

However, the government's demand could be high, and difficulties experienced by individual cultivators could affect the ability of the village estate to satisfy its collective obligations.

Village headmen and influential co-sharers could acquire considerable importance in revenue administration. Their interests did not always coincide with those of poorer cultivators.

The requirement to satisfy the government's demand could contribute to indebtedness and pressure on agricultural households, particularly when harvests or agricultural prices were unfavourable.

Difference from the other systems

Under the Permanent Settlement, the zamindar was the principal intermediary and the government's assessed demand remained fixed permanently.

Under Ryotwari, the individual cultivator dealt directly with the government.

Under Mahalwari, the village or revenue estate was the main unit of settlement, and the village headman or recognised representatives arranged payment. Like Ryotwari, its assessment could be revised.

Prelims focus

  • 1822: Introduction of the Mahalwari Settlement.
  • Holt Mackenzie: Principal official associated with its introduction.
  • 1833: Important subsequent modification under Lord William Bentinck.
  • Initial region: North-Western Provinces of the Bengal Presidency.
  • Mahal: A revenue estate consisting of a village or group of villages.
  • Trap: Mahalwari assessments were periodically revisable, not permanently fixed.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, section A New System Is Devised, printed p. 29, 2020–21 edition in GPSC Volume 04; Drishti IAS, Land Revenue Systems in British India, section The Mahalwari System, published 7 December 2020, consulted 20 November 2026; University of Delhi, Department of Distance and Continuing Education, Colonialism and Nationalism in India, Lesson 5.3.3, Mahalwari Settlement, printed p. 42, course material approved in 2022, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Individual field assessments combined into the revenue demand of a mahal.

title: Mahalwari Settlement of 1822: Revenue Assessment through the Village Community

body:
Why the systems differed across regions

British officials introduced land revenue arrangements at different times as Company territories expanded. They did not replace every existing system with a single model.

Differences in landholding practices, the role of landlords, village institutions and the government's desire for revenue influenced the choice of settlement.

The Permanent Settlement remained especially associated with Bengal, while the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems became important in territories brought under British control during the 19th century.

Principal regional associations

RegionPrincipal systemImportant qualification
Bengal and BiharPermanent SettlementAssociated with the 1793 settlement and zamindari estates.
Madras PresidencyRyotwariDirect settlement with individual cultivators developed extensively.
Bombay PresidencyRyotwari and related survey settlementsRevenue assessed with reference to cultivators' holdings; local practices varied.
North-Western ProvincesMahalwariVillage or revenue estate formed the settlement unit.
Parts of PunjabMahalwari-type arrangementsVillage-based settlements were important, with regional variations.

These are broad historical associations. They should not be interpreted to mean that every district of a presidency followed exactly the same settlement rules throughout British rule.

Land revenue arrangements in Gujarat

Present-day Gujarat did not form one uniform administrative territory under British rule. Its regions had different political histories, including directly administered British territories and princely states.

Parts of Gujarat belonged to the Bombay Presidency, where survey-based land revenue arrangements associated with the wider Ryotwari tradition were important.

Historical land revenue administration in British-administered areas of Gujarat used survey and settlement procedures under the Bombay Land Revenue Code. Land assessment considered factors such as the nature of the land, cultivation, agricultural output, local conditions and other characteristics of the settlement area.

Official Gujarat revenue-administration records identify areas within present-day districts including Ahmedabad, Kheda (formerly Kaira), Surat, Valsad (formerly Bulsar) and Panchmahals as having a connection with the Bombay Presidency's survey-and-settlement arrangements.

This does not mean that the whole of each present-day district necessarily belonged to British-administered territory during the colonial period.

Princely states and other territories

Other areas of present-day Gujarat belonged to princely states or had distinct administrative histories. These included territories associated with Saurashtra and Kutch.

Such regions cannot automatically be classified as Ryotwari merely because they are now part of Gujarat. Their revenue arrangements have to be understood in relation to the political authority and administrative system that applied to each territory.

Gujarat connection: The Bombay Presidency's survey-based revenue administration is relevant to the history of parts of Gujarat, but no single British land revenue settlement should be assumed to have covered all the territories of present-day Gujarat.

Why regional differences affected rural society

Bengal

The Permanent Settlement strengthened the position of zamindars as principal estate-level revenue payers. The government demand remained fixed, while cultivators could face substantial rent demands and insecure tenancy.

Madras and Bombay regions

Under Ryotwari arrangements, the government assessed individual cultivators directly. This removed the zamindar from the principal revenue relationship but exposed cultivators to government assessments, revenue officials and the need to obtain credit.

Northern and northwestern regions

Under Mahalwari arrangements, revenue responsibility was organised around villages or groups of villages. The village headman and recognised co-sharers consequently occupied important positions in revenue administration.

The regional outcome depended not only on the name of the settlement but also on the level of the revenue demand, agricultural conditions and the rights of those occupying the land.

Prelims focus

  • Bengal and Bihar: Principal association with the Permanent Settlement.
  • Madras and Bombay Presidencies: Major regions associated with Ryotwari.
  • North-Western Provinces: Principal early region of Mahalwari.
  • Punjab: Important region of village-based Mahalwari arrangements.
  • Gujarat: Parts of the present state historically belonged to the Bombay Presidency; other areas had different administrative histories.
  • Trap: Modern state boundaries do not necessarily correspond to the territories governed by one colonial revenue settlement.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8 History, Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, printed pp. 28–30, 2020–21 edition in GPSC Volume 04; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Theme 9, section 3.2, printed pp. 247–248, online 2024–25 edition consulted 20 November 2026; Office of the Principal Accountant General (Audit-II), Gujarat, Manual of Audit Management Group-II, Chapter 5, section 5.23.1, History of Land Revenue Assessment, printed p. 162, first edition, official online copy consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Regional Distribution of Land Revenue Systems and the Gujarat Connection
